AI content is low effort content created on the basis of valuable content based on hundreds of hours of human work. Often, it is not based on sources and links because, for example, Open AI does not provide sources of works on which it was learned.

Even if it is good and substantive, it is still based on human work. Therefore, AI content should be depreciated compared to human content because it always has less value due to the impossibility or problematic nature of verifying sources and the risk of possible hallucinations contained in the text, which are sometimes difficult to detect.

Imagine a situation where, while looking for confirmation of whether what is in one text is true, you come across 10 other texts generated by AI with the same nonsense and you become convinced that you are reading the truth and there are no real sources

That is why it is so important to catch it and distinguish it from human content, because there is a risk that search results will be flooded with content fully generated by AI, which generally is often better written in terms of grammar and SEO, which paradoxically translates into a lower search position for content written by humans. . Isn't it about us all drowning in the hallucinations of an algorithm that will soon start learning from variations of its own sweats?

Hello. May I express my opinion here?

I think the two proposed taggings are good ideas, but they seems to be catering to different uses cases and one isn't a substitute to another.

1. `<meta name="author" content="ChatGPT" ai="1">` can be useful for attributions to the AI model generating the contents. I expect the main uses to this are for the AI models themselves, (a.) to avoid feeding with data generated by itself for training lest it causes a loop in data sources, (b.) to makes AIs aware the contents might be generated by a rival AI, and if that rival AI is subject to legal issues (copyright & IP infringements, or contain illegal content otherwise), other AIs that are fed with this data might be legally liable, too.
2. `<meta name="ai-generated" content="all | css-selectors...">` is for more precise tagging of which content is human made and which content is AI. I expect the main uses are browsers and search engines: (a.) browsers may have the motive to visually highlight the text, picture, or videos as AI generated (such as having an AI icon on the corner of the image, or highlight the text with a different color for analysis); (b.) browsers and search engines might implement a filtering techniques of users who want less AI-generated content within their search results.

So the use cases of the two different proposed tagging don't overlap, and we can go with both.

I like this, but I worry the phrase "ai-generated" might become out of date / too vague / meaningless (if it hasn't already) – i.e. at some stage it becomes essential to specify the *type* of AI, or there is some future leap beyond current LLMs.  

Nostalgically, I also like the idea of reusing the term "robot" rather than "ai".  I think it's quite fun, friendly terminology (robots.txt and humans.txt are easily understandable concepts).  Maybe you can introduce "hybrid" or something better for partial content. 

Perhaps you encourage people to reuse the crawler's User Agent string (including version number) when specifying the precise author.

I think the other consideration is audio - and to have a way of distinguishing (I don't believe there already is one) between:

- an audio version of an article read by a real human
- an audio version that was auto-generated
- an item such as a podcast episode page where the audio is in fact the _original_ content and the transcript is either human generated or AI transcribed.

Again, this is all partly to assist crawlers and avoid them needlessly crawling or transcribing ai-generated or simply duplicate material.

My belief that the main purpose of tagging AI content is to satisfy laws that require such labeling. Thus, a generic "AI" label is necessary.
When the contents are labeled as AI-generated, it means the contents may be inaccurate, misleading, or are deliberately forged. In this use case, there is no need to indicate which kind of AI generates them.

Any reason for not just making this a global attribute like `lang`, `role` or `spellcheck`?
Defining a list of elements up-front in a meta tag seems weird and I feel like it'd just encourage authors to set it to ".ai-generated" and then use that class in the same way that you would use a global attribute.
Making this an attribute also means that any technology that wants to determine what content is AI-generated does not need an entire CSS selector matching engine to do so.
To me it seems like this would simplify both the authoring process and the reading of what content is made by AI.

I also think the per-element categorization is definitely needed, otherwise any site with dynamic content (social media sites, news sites, blogs, stores...) would just want to set all their pages to "partial", on the off-chance that ChatGPT gets quoted in an article or an AI-generated post or image comes up. Setting author information at the top of a page only really makes sense if it's a single document that is attributable to a limited number of authors. But many websites are dynamic collages of different things made by countless people and you'd want to tag all that on a case-by-case basis.

My 10^-1.7 cents:

[Unicode's T extension to BCP 47](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/#BCP47_T_Extension) already provides almost perfect method to describe machine-generated contents, the catch is that it currently only covers machine translators. For example `en-t-ko-t0-google` can describe an English content machine-translated from Korean with Google Translate. Given that AI-generated contents can be thought as a transformation from prompts to outputs, a new "Machine Generation" key (likely `g0`) can be introduced to cover this case, so that `en-t-und-g0-chatgpt` would describe an English content generated by ChatGPT. This method alone doesn't cover human-generated contents, but `g0` can be extended to cover this case by having a dedicated value like `none` to describe the absence of machine involvements (e.g. `en-t-und-g0-none`).

@lifthrasiir Machine translation is a different use case from general, AI generated content. Even though the two uses have significant overlap, I don't think one spec is a substitute of another.

Besides, there can be human-and-AI co-authored content, what to do with that?

> [@lifthrasiir](https://github.com/lifthrasiir) Machine translation is a different use case from general, AI generated content. Even though the two uses have significant overlap, I don't think one spec is a substitute of another.

The spec describes various text transformations. One other example is that it has a way to mark the text as transformed by a certain keyboard. AI generation could be added as another type.

Then again, this is for language tags and pictures, even AI-generated ones, aren't necessarily in a language but should be markable.

> Besides, there can be human-and-AI co-authored content, what to do with that?

Any element can have its own `lang` attribute.

> Besides, there can be human-and-AI co-authored content, what to do with that?

The human author simply chooses to declare the content human-authored or machine-authored. I don't like multiple levels of machine authority because no boundaries between those levels are absolutely clear, so having the absolute minimum number of levels (human-authored or machine-authored) seems clearest to me.

Alternatively though, if the middle ground is truly required, the T extension also offers the hybrid locale identifier `h0` which meaning can be extended in the presence of `g0`. For example `en-t-und-h0-hybrid-g0-chatgpt` may mean an English content which has been partly generated by ChatGPT, since it can be thought as a hybrid of `en` and `und-g0-chatgpt` (not the valid tag). I'm not sure this somewhat liberal interpretation of `h0` is acceptable in CLDR, though. I'm just saying that there might be a possible solution in this particular framework.

The upcoming EU AI Act requires companies to declare, when they use AI. That to my understanding also includes translations generated by AI (e.g. DeepL)!

It would be great if we had an HTML attribute to show which parts of the website have been generated using AI. Making a distinction between fully AI generated (complete texts) or partially AI generated (e.g. AI translation of a human-written text) would also be reasonable.

Another advantage is that browsers (or browser extensions) can highlight AI-generated content accordingly or even offer an AI-free mode which hides all AI-generated content if the user doesn't want to see it.
